newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire cabinet urges calm, rush for flights out.
newsitem.headline: Zaire cabinet urges calm, rush for flights out.

text.p: Zaire's government urged the capital not to panic on Monday in the face of relentless rebel advances but travel agents reported a rush of flight bookings by Zaireans trying to flee the spreading civil war.

A statement, issued after an emergency cabinet meeting, said that the battle for Zaire's strategic third city of Kisangani had sparked the rumours, adding that the city had fallen on Saturday to well-armed Ugandan troops.

One minister told Reuters that President Mobutu Sese Seko had telephone twice during the cabinet meeting from his hospital bed in Europe, where he has spent most of his time since prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August.

"The situation created following the battle for Kisangani has given rise over the past 48 hours to all sorts of speculation, particularly in Kinshasa where fanciful rumours have circulated both about the president's state of health and the security of people and property in the capital," it said.
"The government invites the people not to panic as this is both unjustified and fed by pure rumour."
Travel agents, however, reported a post-weekend rush to book seats on flights out of the country. Planes to Europe and South Africa, where Zaireans need no visa, were the most popular.
In Kinshasa's central market, traders prepared to transfer their goods to safe houses, anticipating the mayhem that has regularly occurred after rebels have defeated the army.
"It's the habit of our soldiers to start looting so we have to take precautions," one said.

Residents in Kisangani say that the city, headquarters for army operations in the war zone, fell to rebels after Zairean soldiers looted what they could and fled. Hundreds of defeated government troops surrendered their arms to rebels on Monday.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has called for face-to-face talks with Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and has dominated the sprawling and chaotic nation since then. Opponents accuse him of ruining Africa's potentially richest country.
Rumours on Saturday -- in government circles and more widely in the capital -- suggested Mobutu had died.

Kinshasa residents reported sporadic gunshots overnight on Sunday around the teeming capital, where rumours of an imminent coup attempt are rife. In one incident, armed men opened fire from a car in the opposition stronghold of Limete.
Kisangani is strategically perched on the Zaire River which flows west to the capital 1,500 km (900 miles) downstream.
Rebels, welcomed as liberators along their way, swept into its centre almost unopposed on Saturday but said they met stiff resistance on the approaches during the preceeding days.

The fall of the city sent a shudder through some members of the ruling class. "I don't know what to think," one senior government official said. "We don't know whether the troops will obey their commanders."
The Tutsi-led rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple Mobutu. They accused the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
The government, which has accepted a U.N. ceasefire plan, has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading in support of the rebels. All three deny the charge.
